newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso slams critics before protest.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso slams critics before protest.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, bracing for what could be the largest protest of his presidency on Thursday, has strongly defended his government's attempts to reduce poverty.

"The government does not deny there are social problems but it has dedicated all its efforts to reversing the situation," Cardoso said in a statement issued late on Monday after harsh criticism from the Catholic Church.

A document debated over the weekend at the annual assembly of Brazil's National Bishops Confederation (CNBB) accused the government of buying votes from "corrupt" lawmakers and said Cardoso had failed to keep campaign promises to help the poor.
However, a CNBB spokeswoman said the document was drawn up by a research group linked to the confederation and did not necessarily reflect the views of the bishops.

Cardoso's statement slammed the allegations as "false, slanderous towards Congress and insulting to the government" and listed the government's achievements in reducing child mortality and improving Brazil's income distribution.

The criticism from the bishops came as some 1,500 members of the hard-left Landless Movement (MST) began to converge on the capital Brasilia for a demonstration on Thursday at the end of a two-month march across Brazil.
"We hope we get a good response (from the government) because if we don't we can stay camped for a month or two, however long it takes," march organiser Agosi Ansolin said.

The MST says the government's programme to settle landless families on vacant ranches is too slow and has vowed to carry on its controversial and often bloody policy of organising massive invasions of farmland. More than 100 people have been killed in clashes over land during Cardoso's two-year term.
The Roman Catholic church said on Tuesday that at least 58 landless Brazilian peasants and their leaders were killed last year in conflicts over land.

A spokeswoman for the church's Pastoral Land Commission (CPT) said this took the number of deaths in the last 12 years to 979. She said investigators had still to confirm another three deaths last year that could increase the toll.
"In the 1990s, we have seen an ever-increasing porportion of deaths at the hands of the police," she said.
The latest death count by the church was presented to the Brazilian Catholic Bishops Conference holding an assembly in Sao Paulo state.
